title: Ma'n Has Gone His Way and Left Behind
intro: Marwan ibn Abi Hafsa mourns Ma'n ibn Za'ida, a commander celebrated for his generosity who was killed while governing Sistan. The loss first darkens the sun and shakes whole provinces. Then a woman notices the colour and thinness of Marwan’s own body, and a repeated cry opens out to captives, orphans and poets. The final act belongs to a man who once travelled to Ma'n every year and now puts down his saddle.

translation: Ma'n has gone his way and left behind
noble deeds that will neither perish nor be matched.
1.sharh: The dead man is introduced as a traveller who has gone on ahead. What he leaves is beyond the reach both of time and of anyone who might try to equal him.

translation: On the day Ma'n was struck down, the sun itself
seemed draped in coverings of darkness.
2.sharh: Darkness is a cloth thrown over the sun. Mourning has spread so far that even the source of daylight seems to have been dressed for it.

translation: He was the mountain with which Nizar
brought down the mountains of its enemy.
3.sharh: One mountain is made the means of toppling others. The tribe’s strength against formidable enemies depends on the very solidity of the man it has lost.

translation: The frontier posts fell idle for want of Ma'n,
where once he slaked the thirst of spears.
4.sharh: The frontier is pictured through its suddenly idle weapons. The thirsty spear was conventionally quenched in battle, giving its present stillness the force of an absence.

translation: Iraq went dark. What his death brought upon it,
an all-enveloping calamity, threw it into disorder.
5.sharh: The darkness moves from the heavens to a named country. An enveloping calamity upsets the order of life as well as the appearance of the land.

translation: Syria trembled on either side
when the pillar of its might weakened and leaned.
6.sharh: Syria becomes a structure whose two sides shudder with its failing support. A single leaning pillar gives a visible form to an entire region’s insecurity.

translation: Every tract of Tihama came close,
and of Najd, to shifting the morning he departed.
7.sharh: Lowland and upland alike nearly move from their places. Forms of the same Arabic verb join the land’s displacement to the man’s departure.

translation: If the lands are bowed down in awe for him,
once they stood tall through him in pride.
8.sharh: The lands acquire a bearing like a person standing before us. Their present humility and former proud height are two measures of the same man.

translation: On the day death struck Ma'n, it struck
the noblest in deed among the living.
9.sharh: The verb for striking falls twice, once on an individual and once on a whole order of human worth. The following sequence of gifts supplies the evidence for that claim.

translation: All mankind were Ma'n’s dependants
until he went to visit his grave.
10.sharh: To be a man’s dependants is to look to his household for support. Even his burial is called a visit, the gentlest possible end to such an encompassing obligation.

translation: No one setting out in search of kindness intended
to travel to anyone but Ibn Za'ida.
11.sharh: The seeker’s choice of destination has become automatic. Naming the patron by his father makes the family name itself sound like an address.

translation: Gone is the man who shouldered every burden
and whose overflowing bounty anticipated the request.
12.sharh: His gift reaches people before the words of the petition do. Anticipation saves the petitioner both the burden itself and the humiliation of asking.

translation: No delegations ever made for Ma'n’s equal
or set their saddles down in such a courtyard.
13.sharh: The delegation sets out and then unloads. Saddles laid down in a courtyard turn an abstract judgement about generosity into the end of a recognisable journey.

translation: No palms, even of those renowned for gifts, reached
either the right hand of his pair or the left.
14.sharh: The comparison is made hand to hand with men who are already givers. Even his less celebrated hand would be beyond their reach.

translation: His pools of generosity never ran dry,
brimming with bucketful after bucketful,
15.sharh: Grooves worn by repeated visitors would normally lead to a dwindling pool. Here fresh bucketfuls keep the water available to everyone who comes.

translation: belonging to a man of honour who reckoned wealth
wealth only when he shared it with all who sought good.
16.sharh: The two occurrences of “wealth” stand on either side of the act of giving. For the poet, possession only earns its name by passing into other hands.

translation: If only those who gloated had ransomed him,
if only his life had been stretched out long.
17.sharh: The first wish would exchange the gloaters’ lives for his. The second drops the price of the bargain and voices the bare desire for more time.

translation: His treasure was no hoard of gold, but
Indian swords and finely wrought ring-mail,
18.sharh: Opening the treasury reveals a warrior’s equipment. The rings are the interlocking parts of a coat of mail, valued for their workmanship.

translation: and slender, brown spears from al-Khatt,
in which you see suppleness and straightness,
19.sharh: A shaft may bend without losing its true line. The pair of qualities brings the list of arms down to the grain and temper of the wood.

translation: and a reserve of praise that endures,
and virtue in piety by which he won distinction.
20.sharh: The inventory passes from equipment to things that cannot be packed away. Merit and being preferred are cognate words, tying distinction to a moral quality.

translation: Though now, little by little, they have been put to menial use,
fine horses he could not bear to see so used,
21.sharh: The horses go unnamed until the second half. We first hear what has happened to them, the loss of the special treatment Ma'n once insisted upon.

translation: they used to suffer wounds with him as he advanced
with them in relays, and brought them back heavy-laden.
22.sharh: The horses fought in successive bodies. On the way home their loads of spoils give them the look of pregnant animals, as Atwan’s note explains.

translation: They gathered the spoils and brought them home safe,
though they had passed through deaths that went unavenged.
23.sharh: Success is seen from the saddle, as both the taking and the saving of booty. The closing word evokes blood spilt with no one to exact repayment.

translation: Gone on his way is the man through whom you hoped
the stumbles of your fortunes would be forgiven.
24.sharh: The opening words return, but now the loss belongs to an individual in trouble. Ma'n was the person who could lift him after a fall.

translation: You cannot govern the tears of an eye
whose drops insist on falling in streams.
25.sharh: The mourner addresses himself as “you”. His eye acquires an independent will, turning the vast public loss into a failure of command over his own body.

translation: In your innards is a burning thirst of grief,
like the heat of a fire flaring up.
26.sharh: Water pours from his eye, but nothing quenches the heat within. The verb for flaring is followed by its own verbal noun, prolonging the fire in the sound.

translation: It is as though the night after Ma'n joined
other nights coupled to it, and grew long.
27.sharh: One night seems to have been fastened to others end to end. The missing dawn lets the reader feel duration from inside bereavement.

translation: You have left me and my sons a burden of care
and sorrows that will occupy us long.
28.sharh: Grief is the estate bequeathed to the poet’s household. A man once known for what he bestowed can now leave his dependants only his absence.

translation: And a woman who saw that my body and my colour
had both altered since she last knew them
29.sharh: A second observer interrupts the mourner’s account. Having known him before, she can read a change that no description of the present alone would establish.

translation: saw a man whom grief had worn thin
until it injured him and left him impaired.
30.sharh: The verb suggests shaving material off a stick. By the end of the line grief has reached beyond the man’s outline to the soundness of his whole person.

translation: “I see Marwan grown like a slender blade
of Indian steel that has lost its polish.”
31.sharh: The woman names the poet. Indian steel, once gleaming in Ma'n’s treasury, becomes the image of a mourner whose brightness has gone.

translation: I told her, “What you find strange in me
comes of a calamity that wounded and bore down on me.”
32.sharh: His answer goes from the changes she can see to the hurt she cannot see. The calamity is also an agent that has dealt unfairly with him.

translation: The days of death have their reversals,
turning a man from state to state.
33.sharh: Change passes through the wording of the line as well as its subject. One state follows another before the listener has time to settle in either.

translation: After you, people see us as the remnants of an age
that grants our fortunes nothing but destruction.
34.sharh: The word for remnants can be used of a routed force. Losing one man has made a whole family look to the world like the survivors of defeat.

translation: We are like arrows for which time’s ravages
have left neither feathers nor points.
35.sharh: An arrow needs feathers to fly true and a head to strike. Deprived of both, it keeps its shape while losing its purpose.

translation: We used to drink our fill at that pool of yours
and never visit the scant bowls of muddy water.
36.sharh: The full pool of giving has a poor counterpart in water that barely covers the mud. His dependants once had no need to try such supplies.

translation: How my father would grieve for you when gifts
become false hopes and excuses for delay.
37.sharh: A repeated cry of grief opens with the disappointed petitioner. The formula invokes the speaker’s father, enlarging his lament without introducing another episode.

translation: How my father would grieve for you when captives
complain of heavy rings about their shins.
38.sharh: The particular weight of the irons makes a captive’s need palpable. Ma'n had been someone to whom a plea for release could be addressed.

translation: How my father would grieve for you when orphans
go out dishevelled as though they had consumption.
39.sharh: The orphans’ unkempt appearance makes them look ill with a wasting disease. A simile gives neglect a bodily symptom.

translation: How my father would grieve for you when livestock
graze barren ground and waste away there.
40.sharh: The mourning extends to herds and to the people whose livelihood depends on them. A bare pasture makes generosity a question of survival.

translation: How my father would grieve for you in every battle
whose pregnant creatures cast their young in terror.
41.sharh: The flocks of the previous line remain in view. The shock of fighting reaches even unborn young, giving the warrior’s absence a cost beyond the battlefield.

translation: How my father would grieve for you when verses
in praise of a patron have gone to waste.
42.sharh: Poets enter the company of those who depended on Ma'n. Praise might travel to another court and find nobody there who knew what it was worth.

translation: How my father would grieve for you in every crisis
when men in council ask for some way out.
43.sharh: The last need is for counsel. Those speaking together in confidence need a way through a difficulty that gifts alone could never solve.

translation: We stayed in al-Yamama when hope ran out,
to stay without a wish to leave.
44.sharh: A place name puts a stop to the journeys of petitioners. The verb for staying is followed by its own noun, settling the household ever more firmly in place.

translation: We said, “Where can we journey after Ma'n,
now that bounty is gone and no bounty remains?”
45.sharh: The question gives the reason for staying. Bounty is first pictured departing like its giver, then looked for and found nowhere.

translation: Though you go, many a troop of horses
grim in the fight has checked other troops at your hand.
46.sharh: The horses wear the grim expression of battle-weary fighters. The repeated word for mounted detachments sets one advancing body against another.

translation: To one people you were appointed their spring,
to another the punishment that made an example.
47.sharh: Spring feeds and revives a people. For their opponents, the very same man was a punishment memorable enough to deter whoever came next.

translation: No one who saw battle was more resolute than you,
nobler in stock or stronger of heart.
48.sharh: The three claims concern decision in action, ancestry and courage. They follow the remembered engagements as though the fighting itself could testify.

translation: The caliph will remember you without aversion
when he puts men to the test in affairs of state.
49.sharh: The caliph’s affection has a practical occasion for returning. Trying other men in difficult offices will remind him what Ma'n could do.

translation: He will not forget your engagements, which
brought ruin down upon his enemies,
50.sharh: The engagements are remembered by their consequences for the caliph’s opponents. The sentence carries across the verse boundary towards a particular field.

translation: or a battlefield where you stood guard over honour
when its own horsemen shrank from combat.
51.sharh: The other horsemen’s reluctance brings Ma'n’s decision into focus. His motive is the duty to defend what has been entrusted to him.

translation: A man of Umayya has made you a gift of elegies
alongside the praises he once composed.
52.sharh: The Umayyad affiliate is Marwan himself. Verse reverses the usual direction of a patron’s gift, adding elegies to the praises once brought in person.

translation: He stays home, though every year on his way to you
he used to spend long hours clutching the saddle’s pommel.
53.sharh: Years of trips to the patron survive in the gesture of a hand holding fast to the saddle. The heavy equipment now belongs to a life the poet has left behind.

translation: Grieving, he put down his saddle and swore
an oath never to fasten travelling straps again.
54.sharh: Earlier the delegations unloaded at Ma’n’s courtyard. The poet lays his saddle down at home. The feminine pronoun in the recitation may point back to his oath. In Atwan’s text the masculine pronoun points to the saddle.

1.1.3.head: مَعنُ بنُ زائِدَة
1.1.3.meaning: Ma'n ibn Za'ida al-Shaybani, a commander and governor renowned for generosity, killed in Sistan.

2.2.3-4.head: جِلال
2.2.3-4.meaning: Coverings draped over a body, originally animal cloths. The sun wears them as mourning.

3.1.5.head: نِزار
3.1.5.meaning: Nizar, ancestor of a large grouping of Arab tribes, here the tribes themselves.

4.1.2.head: ثَغر
4.1.2.meaning: Frontier posts guarding the approaches to a territory.

4.2.4.head: الأَسَل
4.2.4.meaning: Spears, with an association of long, slender shafts.

4.2.5.head: نِهال
4.2.5.meaning: Thirsty for a first drink, personifying the spears.

5.2.2.head: مُجَلِّلَة
5.2.2.meaning: Grievous and all-enveloping, said of a calamity.

6.2.4.meaning: Gave way or lost its strength, like an unsound support.

7.1.3.head: تِهامَة
7.1.3.meaning: Tihama, the lowlands along the Arabian side of the Red Sea.

7.2.2.head: نَجد
7.2.2.meaning: Najd, the uplands of the Arabian interior, paired with low-lying Tihama.

8.2.5.head: اِختِيال
8.2.5.meaning: Proud bearing or swagger, attributed to the lands themselves.

9.2.4.head: فَعال
9.2.4.meaning: Worth as shown in action, particularly magnanimous conduct.

10.2.5.head: عِيال
10.2.5.meaning: Dependants whose upkeep a person undertakes.

11.1.4.head: العُرف
11.1.4.meaning: Beneficence or a favour sought from a generous person.

12.2.3.head: نائِل
12.2.3.meaning: A gift, the bounty that reaches the petitioner.

13.2.4.head: رِحال
13.2.4.meaning: Camel saddles. Unloading them marks the end of a journey.

15.2.3.head: مُترَعَة
15.2.3.meaning: Filled to the brim, like the imagined pools of generosity.

15.2.4.head: سِجال
15.2.4.meaning: Large bucketfuls drawn from a well.

16.1.1.head: أَبيَض
16.1.1.meaning: A traditional description of someone of unstained honour and generous character.

16.2.3.head: بُغاة
16.2.3.meaning: Seekers, people who come in search of a benefit.

17.1.4.head: فَدى
17.1.4.meaning: Ransomed him, here by offering themselves in his place.

18.2.3.head: الحَلَق
18.2.3.meaning: Interlocking rings, hence a coat of mail.

18.2.4.head: المُذال
18.2.4.meaning: In Atwan’s gloss, a coat of mail of fine, careful workmanship.

19.1.3.head: الخَطِّيّ
19.1.3.meaning: Khatti spears, named for al-Khatt on the eastern Arabian coast.

21.1.5.head: أُذيلَ
21.1.5.meaning: The horses have been put to common labour, a loss of their former standing.

22.2.2.head: عُقَب
22.2.2.meaning: In relays, with successive groups of horses taking their turns.

22.2.4.meaning: Pregnant. Horses laden with spoils are being likened to pregnant animals.

23.2.5.head: الطِّلال
23.2.5.meaning: In the edition’s gloss, blood spilt without retribution.

24.2.5.head: أُقيلَ
24.2.5.meaning: Be forgiven or remedied, the way a fallen man is helped to his feet.

25.2.4.head: اِنهِمال
25.2.4.meaning: An unbroken flow, of tears as of rain.

26.1.4.head: غَليل
26.1.4.meaning: A burning inward thirst, here the heat of grief.

27.2.3.head: قُرِنَ
27.2.3.meaning: Were yoked or joined together, said of successive nights.

29.2.5.head: حالَ
29.2.5.meaning: Both changed, referring to his body and its colour.

30.1.3.head: بَرى
30.1.3.meaning: Whittled him down, made him thin by degrees.

30.2.4.head: خَبال
30.2.4.meaning: Impairment or debility affecting body or mind.

31.2.2.head: الهِندِيّ
31.2.2.meaning: Hindi, a blade of Indian steel, traditionally prized.

31.2.5.head: صِقال
31.2.5.meaning: The finish or polish on the face of a blade.

32.2.3-4.head: أَنكى وَعالَ
32.2.3-4.meaning: Inflicted a deep hurt and bore unjustly upon him.

33.1.2.head: المَنون
33.1.2.meaning: Death as the power that brings a lifetime to its end.

34.1.4.head: فَلّ
34.1.4.meaning: The remnant of a defeated force, a figure for the people he leaves behind.

35.2.5.head: نِصال
35.2.5.meaning: Arrowheads, the metal points that give arrows their effect.

36.2.3.head: المُصَرَّدَة
36.2.3.meaning: Scantily supplied with water, giving only a meagre drink.

36.2.4.head: السِّحال
36.2.4.meaning: Watering places or their muddy remnants in the edition’s explanation.

37.1.1-2.head: لَهفُ أَبي
37.1.1-2.meaning: “My father’s grief”: an exclamation of lament repeated through seven verses.

37.2.4.head: اِعتِلال
37.2.4.meaning: Putting someone off with excuses. Atwan’s verse has a dotted ghayn, while his gloss gives i'tilal, delay. Al-Basri and Ibn Khallikan also read i'tilal.

38.2.3.head: ساق
38.2.3.meaning: At their shins. Aswuq is a plural of “leg”.

39.2.2.head: أَشعَث
39.2.2.meaning: Dishevelled, with hair unkempt for lack of care.

39.2.5.head: سُلال
39.2.5.meaning: Consumption, a disease that wastes the body.

40.2.1.head: قَرا
40.2.1.meaning: Searched the ground for such grazing as remained.

41.2.4.head: سِخال
41.2.4.meaning: Lambs and kids, here young cast by their mothers before term.

42.2.1.head: مُمتَدَح
42.2.1.meaning: The recipient of a poem of praise.

43.2.3.head: النَّجِيّ
43.2.3.meaning: Confidants speaking privately, a form that can stand for a group.

44.1.2.head: اليَمامَة
44.1.2.meaning: Al-Yamama, a region of central Arabia where Marwan grew up.

44.2.5.head: زِيال
44.2.5.meaning: Removal or departure from a place.

46.1.4.head: رِعال
46.1.4.meaning: Detachments of horsemen, particularly the foremost bodies.

47.2.5.head: نَكال
47.2.5.meaning: An exemplary punishment intended to deter others.

49.1.4.meaning: One who bears aversion or hatred.

49.2.5.meaning: Put men to the test, tried their abilities.

51.1.4.head: حِفاظ
51.1.4.meaning: In defence of an obligation, honour or trust.

52.1.2-3.head: أَخو أُمَيَّة
52.1.2-3.meaning: “A man of Umayya”: Marwan, whose family had been clients of the Umayyads.

53.2.2-3.head: واسِطُ الرَّحل
53.2.2-3.meaning: The front projection of a camel saddle, held by someone spending long hours on the road.

54.1.4.head: آلى
54.1.4.meaning: Swore an oath, reinforced by the noun at the start of the next half.

54.2.4.meaning: “For it”, feminine as heard, can refer to the oath that keeps him from fastening travelling straps. Atwan prints the masculine, referring directly to the saddle.
